transcript:
Hello everyone and welcome to Investing by the Books, a podcast by Radai.
I'm your host, Edipamian, and for this episode we're thrilled to have Chris Mayer back on the show.
Chris is a thoughtful US-based investor, running the fund Woodlockhouse Family Capital.
He is also the author of multiple books on investing and semantics.
And in episode 13, almost five years ago, we discussed his classic title, Hundred Baggers,
about stocks that return 100 times your money, and in many cases much more than that.
I'm a big fan of Chris's style as an investor and also how he writes.
And the other year I did a Swedish translation of his book, Hundred Baggers,
and in connection with that translation, I asked him,
do you have any plans of ever releasing another investing book?
At first it was a no, and then he said,
hmm, I got an idea, but that requires someone to help me.
When I replied, well, I could help you, and he said,
you want to? Sure, you can do it.
And now more than two years later, the idea is taking physical form.
As a book called The Investor's Odyssey about Chris' many lessons on how to survive
the journey of being an investor with all the temptations and detours along the way.
The Investor's Odyssey would be published by Partners Media in the summer of 2026.
We're thrilled to have the author on the show today.
Here comes our conversation with Chris Mayer.
Hi Chris and welcome to Investing by the Books Podcast.
Hello Eddie, it was good to be back on with you.
Great to have you back.
Where are we reaching you this time?
I'm in my home office now finally, so I have been traveling a bit,
but I am in the little town, Mount Erie, Maryland.
Beautiful. And since I know that you like both philosophy and semantics,
I like to start by asking you how long you consider yourself to have been an investor
when was your day one, Subsea?
Yeah. I think my day one is when I bought my first individual stock.
So what I was a late teenager because my dad was and still is an investor.
And so he taught me about mutual funds and things.
So early on, that's what I did.
I had some mutual funds and I remember reading about Buffett and stuff in Fortune Magazine.
But I didn't buy my first stock until I was like 22.
And it was funny because it was into it.
And it went up like 10% a week and I sold it.
I thought that was a lot of money, easy money.
But you know, I'm still just learning and starting at that time,
like often my 20s I was reading is about anything you could find about market.
So even stuff like, you know, the chart reading and from that to Ben Graham
and like everything in between.
Took me a little, took me a little quite a while to kind of settle into more of a style.
But yeah, probably since then.
And what pivotal moments led you to become a professional money manager?
Well, for a long time, I didn't really,
I didn't have any particular ambition to be a professional money manager
because I remember I didn't want to do the whole asset gathering game
and didn't want to deal with, you know, investors blowing in and out at different times.
That whole Wall Street game never appealed for me for a long time.
And even when I was writing my newsletter and I had good track record for a while doing that,
I did get a couple of interesting opportunities to manage money.
But again, it wasn't quite the right setup.
It was always, yeah, you know, more of a traditional asset manager
where you're really spending a good bit of time on the road,
either trying to raise assets or, you know, doing silly updates
with institutional investors that you have.
And so, yeah, I resisted it for a long time.
I just enjoyed investing and I was enjoying the writing life and traveling
and learning about companies.
But then eventually what happened was that the publisher of my newsletter
as a Gora was a Gora.
I was mostly owned by the Bonner family.
So I got to know them well.
And I worked with the Bonner family office in 2016 to start it too.
That was the first time where I really started to get interested.
And then, because the Bonners are perfect partners, our perfect partners.
You know, they've got that patient long-term outlook.
And so that's where I thought, well, this is a case where if I'm ever going to do it,
this would be the setup.
So that's how Woodlock House came about.
And that started on 2nd of January 2019, right?
2019, yeah.
And they seeded it with 25 million to start.
And I remember thinking that might be the only investor I have.
And yeah, it's worked out.
It's grown.
We've got more investors.
And so, yeah, it's been a good journey.
And last time you were on the podcast, we discussed $100.
That was in December 2021.
So what has happened in your life since then almost five years ago?
Well, in 2022, I published another book with the Institute of General Semantics.
It's kind of a hobby interest in mine.
It's called Dear Fellow Time Binder.
I'm also served on the Board of Trustees for that organization,
which aims to promote and publish the Alfred Krizipski's ideas on General Semantics.
So that's more of a, you think of it as kind of a toolkit or system
for critical thinking.
So yeah, I have an interest in that.
So I continue to work with them.
And yeah, let's see what else in the last five years.
I was now on the board of a publicly traded company.
So that's been an interesting thing as well on the board of Technion and Sweden.
But otherwise, yeah, life's the same.
You know, writing the fun, traveling, writing, thinking, all the good things.
Great. And something that has happened as well is that you have been working on a new book.
This one. And it's called The Investors Odyssey.
Right.
So can you briefly explain what is the book about?
Yeah, it's a, it's a book really about long-term investing.
And what I mean is, you know, like really owning, if you're going to own a company,
you know, there's lots of distractions, there's lots of things that pull you away from that goal.
And so I had the idea that, you know, it's kind of like investing is a very long journey
with all these challenges and obstacles and distractions along the way.
So the Odyssey is kind of a good metaphor for that.
So that's kind of the provided kind of the, you know, the basic framework.
And so that's what it is.
That's a kind of steps through what it, what it takes, what, what becomes more important
if you have that mindset and what sort of falls away.
So a very simple terms, that's what it's about.
And we will go deeper into the book a bit later.
But for those who have read the Hundred Baggers or are familiar with it,
how do you compare that one with this book?
Yeah, I mean, Hundred Baggers was really built off of a study that I did of all the stocks
that had gone up at least a hundred times from, you know, 19,
or was it 62 or to, you know, 2014?
And so I was really focused more on that.
And this book is more, you know, reflections on those results
or those insights that I got at that book and reflections from that
because that book came out and, you know, it's been ten years.
There's been other things that I've learned and thought about since.
And so this is much more of a, I say, more qualitative,
more experiential based kind of extended meditation on that
really long-term investing, you know, decade plus of owning a company.
You've dedicated the book to Chuck Akra, who's also the man behind the forward of the book.
So who is Akra and what has he meant for you?
Yeah, Chuck is the founder of Akra Capital Management,
and he's a great investor himself.
He's the one who kind of, he was the one who alerted me to a hundred to one in the stock market,
which was Thomas Phelps' book in 1972.
And that was a book that studied stocks that had gone up at least a hundred to one,
and at that time I had never heard of the book when Chuck introduced it to me.
That was like in 2011.
So yeah, I've learned a lot from Chuck besides that,
because that book was, of course, very important, because then I,
you know, I loved that book, and I would quote from it,
and then I had someone suggest me, oh, you should update it.
I thought, wow, you know, that's a great idea.
So that was important, but I've stayed in touch with Chuck,
and he's kind of been a great mentor from a far.
You know, I've learned a lot from studying his career now.
He invests, and I would say, you know, outside of Buffett Munger,
who influenced probably, probably number one for most people who are investors,
but I'd say Akrae was probably the most impactful.
And I would say, you know, why is that?
Maybe he's worth pointing out that, you know,
one of the things Chuck's really good at and got me to really understand
it took a long time, was this idea of really focusing on the underlying returns
on capital of the business and their ability to reinvest that,
and continue to do it over a long period of time.
And it's basically to strip out a lot of the noise that doesn't affect that core engine.
So that, that, he kind of shifted my focus,
because before that it was much more of a valuation focus,
valuation first sort of investor.
And that's, I think, again, most people go through that phase,
or originally not most, but let's say many investors go through that phase
and they start off with kind of a Ben Graham,
very quantitative style, buying things low price to book, low price to cash flow.
And then, you know, that's a very good approach, works.
And then also as an approach that inherently forces turnover,
because you sell things when they're no longer that cheap,
and you plow it back into things that are cheaper.
And then over time, as you get more capital and more experience,
you kind of, you gravitate more towards wanting to own things for a longer time.
You appreciate the power of compounding.
And this is kind of the old Buffett Munger split, too.
Right? Munger was the one who really kind of came along
and sold Buffett on the idea of buying these higher quality companies
and owning them for a very long period of time.
So that's kind of how Chuck's played that role for me, too.
And the moment you discovered him,
and the Phillips book was in 2011 when he had a speech in Omaha,
that was called an investor's Odyssey.
So besides the speech, what relationship do you have
with the original Odyssey Epic?
When did you first read it?
That's a good question.
Well, I first read it in college,
because I took a class on classics.
So I read it then.
It was the Fitzgerald translation,
which was the most popular then.
And yeah, I've always liked it,
and you see it play out again, again,
again, again, movies, stories,
borrow that basic framework.
And sometimes it's very, you know,
it's kind of intentional and obvious.
Like I remember there's a movie,
O'Brotherware Art thou,
I think it was called with George Clooney and others.
And that's a very, you know, a movie that's obviously built
on the Odyssey's framework.
But it recurs, you know, all through our culture.
And it makes a, it has had a big impact.
And I love the story.
So yeah, and then I read it a couple of times since
there's been different other translations that have come out
and made a splash.
So, you know, Robert Fagel's translation came out.
Like I think it was late 90s.
I remember reading that.
And that was my favorite for a long time.
And every once in a while,
someone comes out, you know,
I'm Emily Wilson's translation.
I forget when that came out,
but that made a splash,
because she kind of really tightened up the language.
And so, yeah, it's,
and I just love the, you know,
I love Greek philosophy and the whole,
all things.
So the Homer's poems, both the Odyssey
and Ilya are very important for like Plato
and those ancient philosophers.
And now there's a book about investing
called the Investors Odyssey.
And this book begins on a plane to Omaha
about 10 years ago when you met an outstanding investor.
So, who was that?
And why does the book begin with this story?
Yeah.
I mean, I think most people wouldn't necessarily think of her
as an outstanding investor initially,
but that's kind of the point.
So, yeah, I met this woman on a plane
and she was,
we were headed to Omaha for the annual meeting
and I wasn't in business class.
I was in the first row right after business class
and she had got bumped from business class
for some reason.
There was like, you know,
some mishap up there
and so they put her next to me.
And we got the chatting and turns out
she was like an investor in the original Buffett partnership.
You know, in the 50s and she rolled her money
in the Berkshire Hathaway
and she, you know, knew Warren
and she's been to like every meeting
and she's basically just held on to the stock
and she became very, very wealthy over time.
And she lives in Tuckett
and she's like giving away Berkshire shares
to her grandchildren.
So it's kind of a cool story.
But I remember thinking about that a lot
and thinking, wow, you know,
here this lady,
she has an attract record as an investor
that smokes, smokes everybody, you know,
investment manager, professionals and so forth.
But she's not doing any of the things
that people would traditionally associate with investors.
She's not, you know, sweating over quarterly report.
She's not worrying about what the Fed's going to do.
She's not making macro predictions or she's not, you know,
she just bought this stock and held it.
So that got me thinking a lot about, well, you know,
that's kind of an example,
a really good example of that kind of approach.
That, yeah, just buying a really good company
and leaving alone.
So I started to kind of unpack her experience like what,
you know, how could you do that?
And in the book,
there's other parts where we talk about investors
that people don't normally think of investors
like founders of companies like Sam Walton or, you know,
but the Walton family also is an investor
and a business that held it for a very long time.
So there is this way to get very wealthy over time.
And that's what the book is about.
And so that's kind of a great anecdote
to set the scene as a word.
And the first chapter of the book then goes out
to describe how the market throws these kind of stocks around.
And on the stormy seas,
there's a lot of things happening every day
and things seems to be important.
And you already wrote a little bit about this in Hundred Baggers
about drawdowns and volatility
and we discussed it in the episode we did in 2021 as well.
But I know you have studied this more
and how common are these movements now, do you think,
and how are the magnitudes changing?
Yeah, I mean, they're very common.
I mean, there's been a bunch of academic work about this.
There's, you know, best and binder study.
And he did an update I think recently
last 100 years of returns and showed drawdowns.
And so even the very best stocks go through periods
where they lose a third of their value over a ten-month stretch.
It was kind of the average.
Sometimes more, sometimes less.
Even in the bulk investors, obviously there's a,
we have a compilation of a number of charts there
where you can see the drawdowns in some of these big winners
and sometimes they're just credibly severe
even, you know, for NVIDIA and Apple and Meta.
You know, you're talking 50, 60% plus drawdowns
during stretches where they were very successful.
So, you know, Marbleson is another one who's put out paper
and I think May of 2025 on drawdowns
and there's some pretty striking information.
They're not only about individual stocks, but also about funds.
You know, top performing funds having drawdowns of 50% plus
is not uncommon for peak to trough.
So, it seems to be this is a hurdle that you have to get over
if you're going to be a long-term investor in anything.
Obviously, you're not going to be able to hold a business
for ten years even if it's even a great stock for ten years
if you can't suffer those kinds of drawdowns.
That's a big lesson from 100 Baggers, of course, too,
but it's something that I emphasize in this book.
You know, ways to deal with it.
But part of it is also just the expectation
and knowing that this is a common and typical experience.
Which is your worst drawdown?
My worst.
Well, I mean, my worst.
I mean, when I was younger, I made a mistake
in a company that was leveraged
and then also turned out to be doing some funny accounting.
So that drawdown was like 99% pretty much went bankrupt.
And that was a very good lesson to learn.
I was like, again, early 20s.
And I was like $2,000 I had invested in it.
And I lost it all.
I remember thinking, well, you know,
that's my tuition for learning this lesson.
And kept me away from companies that were that levered again.
So, yeah, but, you know, more recently,
I've gotten cut in half on a bunch of names.
So it's happened to me as well.
And the second chapter of the book is titled
Resisting the Sirens.
What do you mean by this?
Yeah, well, again, the Sirens in the Odyssey,
you may remember are the, you know,
these, they have women's head,
and they kind of have, you know, wings
and they fly around and sing and,
and lure these sailors to their,
to the rocks near the island where they're, you know,
to their death, so to speak.
And so it's a kind of a, it's a good metaphor
for all the distractions investors have.
You know, there's a lot of media.
And we're bombarded with it.
I mean, we live in a media-soaked world.
Don't appreciate it.
It's not just, you know, what you see on TV,
but social media and the internet.
And so all of that can,
can be an enormous distraction if you let it.
And you looted to it earlier where, you know,
something important is happening every day.
It makes it feel like.
And so you can't relax in that setting.
You've got to be on top of it.
Things are changing.
Of course, you've got to listen to X Podcasts,
read X Newsletter to get the scoop on how to do it.
But yeah, so resisting the Sirens is chiefly about,
resisting or getting past those distractions.
So what do I mean?
Like the one big one, of course, is,
which forces turnover.
So the market tends to amplify quarterly results.
You know, there's these big reactions around quarterly results.
And it makes it seem like something major has changed
when, you know, you look back then over a long period of time.
That quarter is just a little bump on a chart.
So that's what resisting the Sirens is really about.
Different ways you can not get so sucked up in that sort of game.
And one thing I like in this chapter is a list that you have called
don't do these five things.
Can you share one or two of these don'ts?
Yeah, I mean, one is don't check your stock prices so frequently.
And that's it.
That's always a challenge.
But when you're checking your stock prices every day
or multiple times a day,
it does have the effect of amplifying those movements in your mind.
You know, two to three percent move feel like big moves
and 10 percent up or down a week feel like big moves.
And again, when you stretch over that over a longer time rise
and those little incremental changes don't really matter
very much.
How has that changed for you over time?
Yeah, it's still something I struggle with
because I still look at stock prices every day.
But I try not to.
I mean, I try to look maybe once.
Like I look in the morning, I check the news,
see what's going on.
And sometimes, yeah, I'll check during a day.
How can you not?
You know, if earnings come out, I'm curious.
But I try to stay away from that.
It's difficult, like I say.
But I think that that will help extend your horizon.
I also think another one in that list that I mentioned
is not just so much obsessed over the stocks that you've missed.
So there's always something that's hot.
You know, in every market cycle.
And you may not have it.
So right now, we're recording this.
And you know, semiconductors and memory stocks are really hot.
Like, you know, doubling over the last two months or so.
And if you don't own those, you, you know,
you may feel some pressure to make those changes.
But again, historically, you know, the best stocks don't necessarily
have to be at the front every year.
Every year.
You know, even something like Berkshire Hathaway had, you know,
can have two, three years, four years of, of underperforming index.
Not, not, never mind underperforming the best performing stocks.
So you have to get used to that kind of thing.
You know, stretching out your benchmark and how you judge your investments.
Not thinking of it, you know, weekly, monthly, quarterly event.
Just trying to push it out.
And how do you do that practically?
Well, for me, I think what helps a lot is focusing on the business.
And so what is that being?
That means, you know, there's for every business, there's probably a handful
of really key things that are important.
Might be margins might be reinvestment rate might be.
Some cash flow, you know, definitely cash flow is always important.
Kind of counting cash flow.
And so as long as those things are going well,
or trending the way you want them, the way you expect,
and then you just leave it alone.
And you also have to remember to give your companies kind of a band.
You know, they're going to not going to have their best years every year.
Sometimes you have to allow for, you know, a subpar or a year for that company.
And not sell it.
It was interesting because I recently read a bit of Warren Buffett's letter
from 98 or 99.
And he was, of course, badly trailing the market then.
And he acknowledged in there that several of his companies have had disappointing results.
But he didn't sell them, you know.
They had disappointing results, but he still believed in them long term.
And so I think that's also difficult for investors.
You know, they want to pull out the rip quarter as soon as the company reports a disappointing quarter
or it looks like it might have a subpar a year or two even,
even though the longer term, you know, trend for that company is still in place.
So that's helped me a lot.
Just focusing on those numbers and just not even, you know,
not reacting to the drawdowns, except if you, you know, want to buy more.
That would be the only way.
Then there is always media, as you mentioned,
playing their siren songs.
And you give some thoughts on media consumption
and one part is about paying attention to language.
Why is this relevant for investors, do you think?
Yeah, I mean, I think the language is important
because there are a lot of reasons.
I mean, it makes me think of, you know, how the market
or people when they talk will often paint certain stocks with broad brush.
So right now we're in this period where anything software related is kind of a poison.
But, you know, all software is not the same, right?
There's a lot of differences in software companies,
even though people tend to think of it in the same bucket.
So yeah, that's definitely one.
And just the way you use language, you say things like, you know,
you have to watch your always and your nevers
and being definitive about saying things is, you know, they are a certain way
or this is this way rather than saying, well, it seems to be or seems to me, you know,
allowing variants of opinion or allowing yourself to change your opinion later down the road.
So yeah, language is important.
In that chapter, I draw on some of the stuff that Neil Postman has done.
And so he wrote a great book called, I'm using ourself to death.
But Neil Postman also was very much influenced by Alfred Krasit,
who I mentioned, General Semantics before, and he was involved in the Institute as well.
So kind of ties back nicely.
And later in the book, you describe what a great business looks like to you,
how to think about operators and what the best companies do with their profits.
And in recent years, you've been a frequent participant at Red Eyes Series
conference here in Stockholm, and you've invested in a couple of Swedish companies
and are on the board of one of them, as you mentioned.
How has your view on these so-called serial inquiries evolved over these years?
Yeah, I mean, I like the serial inquire model.
I mean, it's a main attraction.
Is it solves that reinvestment part of the equation?
You know, there's two components to generating good results over a long time.
You need that high return on capital, but then ideally,
you want to be able to reinvest and continue to generate good returns.
And so the serial inquires are built to solve that problem, basically.
And that's their focus is getting good returns and then reinvesting it at good returns
and continuing to do that time and time again.
So it's a great model.
And there are a lot of different flavors and styles to do it.
You know, you can then be focused on a verticalical.
You can go across many different kinds of companies.
Some use more debt.
Some use less.
Some issue shares.
Some don't.
Some buy 100% of the companies they buy.
Some only buy 80% of the companies they buy.
So there's a lot of little particulars once you get into it.
You can appreciate the different flavors and styles.
And they can all be successful in different ways.
So, yeah, my thinking, I don't know how it's evolved.
I guess there's just been more refinements around certain things.
I would say, you know, I pay more attention now to sort of process
and the internal structure and controls and those sort of boring issues
that investors don't often think about.
But those kinds of things provide the foundation for success.
You can have zero acquires who put up good numbers for a while,
but they don't really have that infrastructure in place to deal with,
you know, when they get, when they hit bumps in the road.
So that's been something that's evolved over time.
But yeah, it's a good model.
I think there's lots of interesting opportunities there in that space.
I'm sure they need to be investor there for a long time.
And an example in the book is a UK company called Halma.
What's their secret sauce?
Yeah, Halma's secret sauce is really very much the secret.
It's pretty, it's kind of very simple ingredients.
So, you know, they keep the share price, keep an eye on their share count, I should say.
And they are focused on acquiring companies,
but, you know, they're the small, repeatable acquisitions that they do
with their internally generated cash flow overwhelmingly.
So, I think Halma's share count hasn't moved much over a very long period of time
compared to what their increase in cash flow has been.
And yeah, folks in high quality.
And it's like, watch prints repeat.
And they've applied that formula for a long time and very successful.
So, Halma drew my attention because there was a speech that their founders gave
where he could laid out the basic blueprint of what a successful zero acquire looked like.
And that model hasn't changed.
And one benefit with these kind of companies is also the kind of building diversification that they have.
How do you think about that?
Some people see it as a black box because they don't really know what's in there.
What are your thoughts on it?
Yeah, and people who come new to the new to zero acquires,
they have this itch where they want to try to underwrite every company in the portfolio.
I know I appreciate that because I remember when I first came,
I was also asking a lot of questions about individual companies trying to understand them.
But then I realized that's not really the right way to go about it.
You really have to be much more comfortable with the sort of home office, if you will,
their investment philosophy and their style and what they're looking for.
And you have to have trust in them in applying that.
And then other than that, you're really focused on the output, which is the cash flows
and returns and the investments.
And so yeah, you can't really you can't underwrite them, especially as they get larger.
So it's some people are comfortable with that some aren't.
I like that aspect of it too because as you mentioned,
you have that internal diversification.
So it's just harder to, you know, to kill one bullet.
You might have a subsidiary go to zero.
You know, just be a little bump for the company overall.
Versus if you were just in a company that did that one thing,
